title: The Thomas Christians
hookLine: the Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara churches of India trace their faith to Thomas

cards: Kerala, on the southwest coast of India. Coconut palms, backwaters, rain that arrives like a wall. A bride in a gold-bordered sari walks out of a church, and her family has kept the faith for as long as anyone can say.
Ask them where it came from, and they won't say Portugal, or England, or a missionary from Europe. They'll name an apostle. Thomas, they'll tell you.
He came here. Some of their churches carry his name over the door. Today, the people who call themselves his children.

teach.h: LET US ALSO GO, THAT WE MAY DIE WITH HIM.
teach.b: The Gospels show Thomas as more than a doubter. When Jesus decides to go back toward danger in Judea, John's Gospel gives Thomas the brave line: "Let us also go, that we may die with him."
Later, yes, he says he won't believe the resurrection until he touches the wounds. But when he sees Jesus, he says, in the Douay-Rheims, "My Lord, and my God."
Bold, then doubting, then a confession that calls Jesus Lord and God. Then India. The Gospels end before Thomas's travels begin.
Ancient tradition says he sailed east and preached on the Malabar coast, and the Christians of Kerala keep that memory, with places and songs tied to his name.
Scholars debate the history; the families don't need them to settle it to know who they are. Today two Eastern Catholic churches belong to this family.
The Syro-Malabar Church prays in the East Syriac tradition, the Syro-Malankara Church in the West Syriac tradition, and both call their Eucharist the Holy Qurbana.
Not every Thomas Christian is Catholic: Orthodox and other churches share the same heritage, and the same apostle.
What they've kept is a faith fully Indian, at home in a land of many faiths, with customs drawn from their own soil, and fully Catholic too.
The faith wasn't imported, they'd say. It grew here, from a seed an apostle planted.

how: Syro-Malabar Catholics celebrate the Holy Qurbana in the East Syriac tradition and Syro-Malankara Catholics in the West Syriac tradition, mostly in Malayalam; both churches honor Saint Thomas as the apostle who, by their tradition, brought the faith to India.

games.q: you're Thomas. the others tell you they've seen the risen Lord. you weren't there. what do you say?
o: "unless I touch the wounds, I won't believe."
games.why: he demands proof. eight days later Jesus offers his wounds, and Thomas answers "my Lord, and my God."

practice: Picture India from above: mountains in the north, the long coasts, cities full to bursting, villages at dusk, and its Christians living among neighbors of many faiths. Let the whole of it in, without picking favorites.
If you pray, pray for India and all its people, perhaps with Thomas's words, my Lord, and my God; if you don't, wish the whole country well, whatever hour it is there now.

wordCard.voice: The Thomas Christians. The ancient Christians of Kerala, in India, who trace their faith to the apostle Thomas. Two of their churches are Eastern Catholic: the Syro-Malabar and the Syro-Malankara. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: twin. John's Gospel calls him "Thomas, who is called Didymus."
